title: Growing in Virtue: One Psychological Perspective
description: Investigations by the Thomistic Institute Growing in Virtue: One Psychological Perspective Motivation, Mindset, and Means Tim Reilly Nov 23, 2026 11 5 1 Share Nicolas-Henri Jacob, from Bourgery’s “ Traité complet de l'anatomie de l'homme,” 1831–1854, via Wikimedia Commons . In this article, I want to focus on a psychological framework developed by psychologists for thinking about the more general process of growth in virtue. This framework encourages attention to (1) motivation, (2) mindset, and Motivation here is, on the surface, fairly straightforward. If we are to grow in virtue or character, we must desire to grow in that way. Motivation might arise from a recognition that one is focused on avoiding vice more than on pursuing virtue. For instance, thinking to oneself when faced with a challenge—I don’t want to make a mistake—rather than thinking about what the best thing one might do is. … 11 5 1 Share A guest post by Tim Reilly A developmental psychologist studying purpose, vocation, and virtue. He is the author of "Moral and Intellectual Virtues in Practices: Through the Eyes of Scientists and Musicians". Subscribe to Tim Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Liked by Tim Reilly Stephanie Marie 15h So well written! I especially love this quote: “If we can appropriately address the inhibitory fears and desires, we will be more free to pursue growth. This is what growth in temperance and fortitude often is. Even more, the good that we want to grow in is ideally an expression of our desire for justice—we recognize that we ought to be better for God and others.” When I look at my own desire for growth, it’s almost always related to how I relate to other people. Where I can listen better, understand better, show more empathy, love better, etc.

title: Time in Science and Philosophy
description: Investigations by the Thomistic Institute Time in Science and Philosophy Where Physics and Philosophy Meet Jonathan I Lunine Nov 09, 2026 23 1 6 Share Johannes Vermeer, “The Astronomer,: 1668, via Wikimedia Commons. Physicists who work in general relativity carry two very different definitions of time in their research. One is “proper” time, which is a measure of the amount of physical change that a system experiences. Proper time is what a clock measures. Carry a clock from event A to event B, “Coordinate” time, on the other hand, is one of four coordinates assigned to events in the four-dimensional continuum called spacetime. Spacetime consists of three space-like dimensions and one time-like dimension in our universe. The path of any material entity through spacetime can be visualized as a series of events, which are linked together to form its world line. Coordinate time is a labeling of events that allows one to quantify the relationship between different worldlines.
